n: Group candidate features by entity (user, item, context, user-item interaction) and by freshness (static, batch-updated, real-time). The grid makes gaps obvious.
Interaction and aggregate features, such as a user's click rate on a category over 7 days, usually carry most of the signal in ranking and risk models.
Every feature has a cost: computing it, storing it, fetching it within the latency budget, keeping it consistent, and the privacy risk. Add features whose gain pays for that.
High-cardinality IDs can be encoded by hashing, target statistics computed out of fold, or learned embeddings. Each has its own failure mode.
lessons.a:
## Where signal comes from
Most of a model's quality comes from its features. A plain logistic regression with well-chosen features often beats a deep model with poor ones. The design question is which features to compute, how fresh they need to be, and whether each is worth its cost. The Machine Learning course's "Feature engineering" module (mlcore 07) covers transformations such as scaling, encoding and imputation; this lesson is about choosing features at the system level.

## A grid of candidates
Organise ideas along two axes: which entity the feature describes, and how often it changes.
| | Static | Batch (hours to days) | Real-time (seconds to minutes)
| User | country, signup date | purchases last 30 days, preferred categories | items viewed this session
| Item | category, brand, price tier | rating, sales last 7 days | current stock, live price
| Context | | | time of day, device, query, page position
| User-item | | user's past rating of the brand | clicked this item earlier in the session

Filling the grid for a new problem gives a long list quickly and shows gaps. Real-time features are the most expensive to build, so ask whether a batch version would capture most of the signal.

## Aggregates and interactions
The strongest features in ranking and risk models are usually aggregates over windows:
- counts and rates: user's click-through rate on this category over 7 and 30 days;
- recency: time since the user last bought from this shop;
- velocity: number of transactions on this card in the last hour;
- ratios: this price divided by the user's median price.

Use several windows (1 hour, 1 day, 30 days) so the model can separate habits from bursts. Compute them as of the prediction time (01.03) and smooth small counts, for example with a prior, so a user with one view and one click does not get a 100% click rate.

```sql
-- 7-day category click-through per user, as of each impression time
SELECT i.impression_id,
       SUM(c.clicked) * 1.0 / NULLIF(COUNT(c.event_id), 0) AS user_cat_ctr_7d
FROM impressions i
LEFT JOIN events c
  ON c.user_id = i.user_id AND c.category = i.category
 AND c.ts >= i.ts - INTERVAL '7 days' AND c.ts < i.ts
GROUP BY i.impression_id;
```

## High-cardinality categories
User IDs, item IDs, merchants and query strings have millions of values.
- **One-hot** is impossible at that scale.
- **Hashing** maps values into a fixed number of buckets. It is cheap and handles new values, but collisions merge unrelated values.
- **Target statistics** (mean label per value) are powerful but leak unless computed out of fold or from earlier time windows.
- **Learned embeddings** let a neural model learn a dense vector per value. They need enough data per value and a strategy for unseen values (03.04).

## The cost of a feature
| Cost | Question
| Compute | how much work to produce it, and how often?
| Serving latency | can it be fetched within budget at p99?
| Consistency | is it computed the same way offline and online?
| Maintenance | which upstream team owns the data, and will it change?
| Privacy and fairness | is it allowed, and could it act as a proxy for a protected attribute?
| Coverage | what fraction of requests have it, and what happens when it is missing?

A feature that adds 0.2% AUC but needs a new streaming pipeline and a synchronous call to another team's service may not be worth it. Measure each feature's marginal value with ablations or permutation importance, and remove features that do not pay their way. Unused features still cost money and still break.

%%flow A feature's life. Most of the work is after the first experiment shows it helps.
Idea -(offline ablation)-> Proven gain -(build pipeline + online version)-> *Production feature -(monitor coverage + drift)-> Keep or retire
%%

! Example: a feature that hurt in production
! A delivery-time model gained 3% accuracy offline from "restaurant's current queue length". Online, the feature came from a service with 150 ms p99 latency and was missing for 8% of requests, where the model fell back to a default and produced worse estimates than before. A batch feature, "average queue length at this hour of the week", gave most of the gain with no latency and full coverage.

## Missing values
Missingness is common and often informative: a new user has no purchase history. Keep an explicit "missing" indicator rather than silently imputing a mean, and make sure the serving path produces the same default as training. A feature that is missing at a different rate online than offline is a skew bug.

## Pruning
Feature lists grow with every experiment. Review them on a schedule: drop features with near-zero importance, features whose upstream data is being deprecated, and near-duplicates. Fewer features mean faster serving, simpler debugging and fewer ways for a pipeline change to break the model.

> Takeaway: generate features from an entity-by-freshness grid, lean on windowed aggregates and interactions computed as of prediction time, handle high-cardinality IDs deliberately, and keep only features whose gain pays for their compute, latency, consistency and privacy costs.
lessons.q: You are building a model to predict whether a user will book a hotel they view. List features in four groups (user, item, context, user-item), say which must be fresh within minutes, and name one feature you would leave out and why.
lessons.s: User: account age, past bookings in the last year, average nightly price booked, typical trip length, loyalty tier, device. Item (hotel): star rating, review score and count, price for the dates, distance to city centre, cancellation policy, booking rate over the last 30 days. Context: search destination and dates, days until check-in, number of guests, time of day, rank position, filters applied. User-item: has the user viewed or booked this hotel before, price relative to the user's usual price, distance from the user's previously booked hotels. Must be fresh: price and availability for the dates (change minute to minute), the user's activity in the current session, and recent views. Leave out the user's precise home address: privacy risk, little extra signal over coarse region and trip distance, and it is hard to justify. Also avoid any feature only known after booking, such as "booking confirmation email opened".

n: A **feature store** gives each feature one definition and two materialisations: an offline store with history for training and an online store with the latest value for serving.
Its main job is consistency. It removes the risk of training and serving computing the same feature differently, and supports point-in-time joins.
Batch features are computed by scheduled jobs; streaming features by a stream processor; request-time features in the serving path. All three must be defined once.
You do not always need a feature store. Small systems can log served features and share one library of feature code, which solves most of the same problems.
lessons.a:
## The consistency problem
Every model depends on two programs agreeing about features: the one that builds training data and the one that serves predictions (01.03). In small projects one engineer writes both, and the risk is manageable. In a company with dozens of models and hundreds of features, teams reimplement the same feature in different languages, at different freshness, with different edge cases. A feature store is infrastructure to stop that.

## What a feature store does
- **Registry**: one definition per feature, with owner, entity, type, freshness and description.
- **Offline store**: full history of feature values with timestamps, usually in a data warehouse or lake, for building training sets.
- **Online store**: the latest value per entity in a low-latency key-value store, for serving.
- **Point-in-time joins**: given a list of (entity, timestamp) pairs, return each feature as of that timestamp.
- **Materialisation jobs**: compute features from source data and write them to both stores.

%%flow One definition, two materialisations. Training reads history; serving reads the latest value.
Source events -(feature definition)-> Batch or stream job -(timestamped values)-> Offline store -(point-in-time join)-> Training data
Batch or stream job -(latest value)-> *Online store -(get by key, ~ms)-> Serving
%%

## Three kinds of features
| Kind | Computed by | Freshness | Example
| Batch | scheduled job, hourly or daily | hours | user's purchases last 30 days
| Streaming | stream processor | seconds to minutes | card's transactions in last 10 minutes
| Request-time | the serving code | instant | query length, time of day, distance to restaurant

Request-time features are not stored at all; they come from the request. They still need one shared implementation, typically a library used by both the training pipeline (applied to logged requests) and the server.

## Point-in-time correctness
Training data is built by asking the offline store: "for user 42 at 2024-03-01 14:05, what was `orders_7d`?" The store returns the last value written before that timestamp. This prevents future information leaking into training. It needs the offline store to keep history, not just the current value, and to record when each value became available, not only the event time it refers to. Late-arriving data is a common subtle bug: an event from 13:50 that arrived at 14:30 must not be visible at 14:05.

! Example: freshness skew without a code bug
! A feed-ranking team used a daily batch feature for "author's posts in the last 24 hours". Online it was read from the online store, which was refreshed once a day at 02:00. Offline, training used point-in-time joins, but the job that backfilled history had computed values at event time, not at availability time. Training saw a feature that was always current; serving saw one up to 24 hours old. Recording availability timestamps and joining on them removed the gap.

## Do you need one?
A feature store pays off with many models sharing features, streaming features, or several teams. For a single model, two cheaper habits get most of the benefit:
- put feature code in one library imported by both training and serving;
- log the features used at serving time and build the next training set from those logs.

In an interview, name the feature store as the component that guarantees consistency, then say what it stores, how fresh each feature is and what happens on a cache miss.

## Failure handling
The online store can be slow or missing a key. Decide per feature: use a default (and make sure training saw the same default), fall back to a coarser batch feature, or skip the model and use a fallback ranking. Monitor the miss rate as a first-class metric; a sudden rise usually means a failed materialisation job.

## Backfills and new features
When you add a feature, you need its history to train on. A backfill job computes historical values from source data, and it must use the same definition and the same availability rules as the live job, or the new feature will be skewed from day one. Some teams instead start logging the new feature at serving time and wait a few weeks to collect training data, which is slower but guaranteed consistent. Either way, compare the backfilled values with live values for a recent overlap period before trusting them.

> Takeaway: a feature store gives each feature one definition with an offline history for point-in-time training joins and an online store for serving; whether or not you use one, share feature code, record availability times and log served values.
lessons.q: Two teams compute "number of orders in the last 7 days" for a user. The training pipeline uses a nightly SQL job; the serving path increments a counter in a cache on each order. The model degrades for active users. Explain why and design a fix.
lessons.s: The two computations differ in at least three ways. The nightly SQL value is up to 24 hours stale, so at training time the model sees a lagged count, while serving sees a live one; for active users, who order more often, the gap is largest. The cache counter may never decrement orders older than 7 days, or may reset on cache eviction, so it drifts from the true windowed count. Cancelled orders may be excluded in SQL but counted by the increment. Fix: define the feature once, for example in a feature store, as a 7-day window over the order event stream; compute it with a streaming job that writes both to the online store (latest value) and to the offline store (timestamped history). Train with point-in-time joins against the offline history, and log the served value with each prediction so you can measure any remaining mismatch.

n: An **embedding** maps an entity (user, item, query, image, text) to a dense vector so that similarity in the vector space reflects similarity for the task.
**Two-tower** models learn query and item embeddings separately, so item vectors can be precomputed and searched with approximate nearest neighbour (ANN) indexes.
ANN indexes such as HNSW and IVF-PQ trade a little recall for orders of magnitude less latency and memory. Measure recall@k against exact search.
Embeddings go stale and versions are incompatible. Re-embed and re-index when the model changes, and never compare vectors from different model versions.
lessons.a:
## Why vectors
Many systems need to find "things like this" among millions of options: products for a query, songs for a user, images similar to a photo, documents relevant to a question. Comparing raw features pairwise is too slow and does not capture meaning. An embedding model maps each entity to a vector, typically 64 to 1,024 dimensions, trained so that a similarity function (dot product or cosine) is high for pairs that should match.

The AI Engineering course's embeddings module (aieng 02) covers vector databases and index internals in depth; here the focus is design choices.

## Where embeddings come from
| Source | Example | Pros | Cons
| Pretrained encoders | text or image models | no task data needed | not tuned for your notion of similar
| Co-occurrence | items bought together, word2vec on sessions | cheap, captures behaviour | cold start for new items
| Two-tower models | query tower and item tower trained on engagement | task-specific, precomputable | needs lots of interaction data
| Fine-tuned encoders | pretrained model fine-tuned on your pairs | strong with modest data | more training cost

## Two-tower retrieval
A two-tower model has one network for the query side (user, context, query text) and one for the item side. Their output vectors meet only in a dot product: $s(q, i) = u_q^\top v_i$. Because the item tower does not see the query, all item vectors can be computed offline and indexed. At request time you compute one query vector and search.

Training uses positives from engagement (clicks, purchases) and negatives sampled from other items. **In-batch negatives** reuse the other items in a minibatch, which is cheap but over-samples popular items; a **logQ correction** subtracts the log of each item's sampling probability from its logit to remove that bias.

%%flow Two-tower retrieval. Item vectors are built offline; only the query is embedded per request.
Catalogue -(item tower, offline)-> Item vectors -(build)-> *ANN index
Request -(query tower, online)-> Query vector -(top-k search)-> ANN index -(500 candidates)-> Ranker
%%

## Approximate nearest neighbour search
Exact search over 50M vectors of 128 dimensions is 6.4 billion multiply-adds per query: too slow at high QPS. ANN indexes find most of the true neighbours much faster:
- **HNSW** builds a layered proximity graph and walks it greedily. It gives high recall and low latency but uses a lot of memory.
- **IVF** clusters vectors and searches only the nearest clusters.
- **Product quantisation (PQ)** compresses each vector to a few bytes, cutting memory 10 to 100 times at some cost in accuracy.

Tune on **recall@k versus latency**: for a random sample of queries, compare the ANN results with exact search. A recall of 95% at 10 ms is a typical target.

## Memory estimates
Vectors: $N \times d \times 4$ bytes in float32. 100M items at 256 dimensions is about 100 GB, which calls for sharding or compression. HNSW adds graph links, often 1.5 to 2 times the vector memory. PQ at 64 bytes per vector cuts 100M items to about 6.4 GB.

! Example: version mismatch
! A team retrained the item tower and rolled it out by re-indexing items gradually over a day. The query tower was switched immediately. For several hours, queries from the new model were compared against item vectors from the old one, and relevance collapsed for items not yet re-indexed. Versioning the index and switching query and item towers atomically fixed it.

## Keeping embeddings fresh
New items need vectors before anyone can find them. Embed them on creation and add them to the index incrementally; rebuild the full index periodically for balance. When the model changes, re-embed everything and switch index versions in one step. Monitor index size, build time, recall on a fixed query set, and the share of results that are new items.

## Beyond retrieval
Embeddings also make good features for downstream rankers, for clustering and deduplication, and for diversity re-ranking (choose items that are relevant but not too similar to each other). They are compact, but treat them as a versioned artifact: a vector means nothing without the model that produced it.

> Takeaway: train embeddings so that dot products reflect task similarity, use two towers so item vectors can be precomputed, search them with an ANN index tuned on recall versus latency, and version models and indexes together so vectors are never mixed.
lessons.q: You need to retrieve 500 candidate products from a catalogue of 50 million for each search query within 20 ms. Design the embedding and indexing approach, estimate the memory needed, and say how you would keep it up to date.
lessons.s: Train a two-tower model: a query tower (text encoder plus user and context features) and a product tower (title, category, image and attribute features), trained on query-product engagement with in-batch negatives and logQ correction for popularity. Use 128-dimensional normalised vectors and dot-product similarity. Raw float32 vectors take 50M × 128 × 4 bytes = 25.6 GB, which is large but fits in memory on a few machines; with product quantisation to 32 bytes per vector it is about 1.6 GB. Use an IVF-PQ or HNSW index sharded across machines, tuned for recall@500 of about 95% against exact search at under 15 ms. Keep it fresh by re-embedding new or changed products incrementally (append to the index every few minutes) and rebuilding the full index nightly. When the model is retrained, re-embed the whole catalogue with the new product tower and switch query and index versions together.

n: **Cold start** is predicting for users or items with little or no history. Collaborative signals are missing exactly when the first impression matters most.
For new users, use context (location, device, referral source), onboarding questions, and popular or trending items within a segment, then adapt quickly as signals arrive.
For new items, rely on **content features** (text, image, category, price, creator) that map into the same space as established items.
New items need **exploration**: a reserved share of exposure, boosted by uncertainty, so the system can learn about them. Otherwise popular items stay popular forever.
lessons.a:
## Where collaborative signals run out
Recommenders and rankers learn a lot from interaction history: users who liked A also liked B. That signal does not exist for a user who signed up a minute ago or an item listed this morning. Yet these are often the moments that matter most: a new user decides whether to stay, and a new item either gets discovered or sinks. Cold start is a design problem, not just a modelling one, because the fixes involve data collection, exposure policy and evaluation.

## New users
Start from what you do know:
- **context**: country, language, device, time, referral source or campaign, the first search query;
- **onboarding**: a few quick choices ("pick three topics") that seed preferences;
- **segment popularity**: what similar new users in the same context engage with;
- **fast adaptation**: update the user's representation within the session from their first clicks, rather than waiting for the nightly retrain.

Session-based models, which take the sequence of recent actions as input, handle new users naturally because they never needed a long history.

## New items
For items, content is the bridge:
- text (title, description), images, category, price, brand, creator and their track record;
- a **content tower** that maps these into the same embedding space as items with history, trained so its output matches the learned embedding of established items;
- metadata-based similarity to established items ("similar to listings that sold well").

When the item collects interactions, blend toward its collaborative representation.

%%flow A new item's path to a learned representation.
New item -(content features)-> Content embedding -(exploration exposure)-> First interactions -(near-real-time stats)-> *Blended embedding -(enough history)-> Collaborative embedding
%%

## Exploration
A model that ranks only by predicted engagement will rarely show items it is unsure about, so it never learns about them. Popular items get more exposure, more data and higher scores, which is a rich-get-richer loop. Breaking it needs deliberate exploration:
| Strategy | How it works | Trade-off
| Reserved slots | a fixed share of positions for new or low-exposure items | simple, but blind to quality
| Epsilon-greedy | show a random candidate with probability $\epsilon$ | wastes impressions on poor items
| Upper confidence bound | boost items with high uncertainty | needs uncertainty estimates
| Thompson sampling | sample a plausible score from each item's posterior | explores in proportion to the chance of being best
| Contextual bandits (LinUCB) | uncertainty bonus based on features | personalised exploration

The exposure budget is a business decision: more exploration helps new sellers and long-term catalogue health, but costs short-term engagement. State it explicitly, for example "5% of impressions go to items with fewer than 100 impressions".

! Example: a content model that unlocked a catalogue
! A music service found that 60% of newly released tracks were never recommended, because their collaborative embeddings were random until the weekly retrain. Adding an audio-and-metadata tower that predicted the collaborative embedding from content, plus a 3% exploration budget for tracks under a week old, raised new-track exposure fourfold while overall listening time stayed flat.

## Evaluating cold start
Average metrics hide cold-start performance because established users and items dominate the data. Report metrics separately for new users (first session, first week), new items (first day, first week), and established ones. Track coverage: what share of new items get at least some impressions within a day. Offline evaluation with leave-last-out splits overstates quality for new users; simulate cold start by hiding a user's history and scoring their first actions.

## The system around it
Cold start touches several components: onboarding UI, a content embedding pipeline that runs when an item is created, a streaming job that updates item statistics within minutes, and an exposure policy in the ranker. A good design names all four.

## Avoiding a bad first impression
Exploration should not show a new user poor content. Explore mostly with established users who have shown tolerance, cap how many exploratory items appear on one page, and filter candidates by quality signals from the content model before they enter the exploration pool. New users get the safest personalisation available: popular items in their segment, adjusted by their first few actions.

> Takeaway: for new users lean on context, onboarding and fast in-session adaptation; for new items use content features mapped into the same space as learned embeddings, give them a deliberate exploration budget, and measure cold-start performance separately.
lessons.q: A marketplace adds 200,000 new listings a day. Your recommender is a matrix factorisation model retrained nightly, so new listings get no exposure until the next day and many never get any. Propose changes so new listings are shown, learned about and judged fairly.
lessons.s: Give new listings a content-based representation from day one: an item tower that embeds title, photos, category, price and seller history into the same space as the collaborative embeddings, trained so that for established items its output matches their learned vectors. Use it to retrieve new listings alongside established ones. Reserve a small exposure budget (for example 5% of slots) for listings with few impressions, chosen by a bandit such as Thompson sampling on click or conversion rate with a prior from the content model, so uncertain items get tried and good ones rise quickly. Update listing statistics in near real time from a stream so a listing that performs well in its first hours gets more exposure the same day. Evaluate separately for new and established listings, and track the share of new listings that receive at least N impressions within 24 hours, along with buyer conversion so exploration does not hurt overall quality.
